ETES systems can be used to store excess electricity generated by renewable energy sources, such as solar and wind power, and release it when needed to provide energy to the grid. ETES systems typically use resistive heating elements or heat pumps to convert electricity into thermal energy, which is then stored in a thermal energy storage medium, such as molten salt or solid particles. The stored thermal energy can be used to generate electricity on demand by running it through a heat engine, such as a Rankine cycle or a supercritical carbon dioxide cycle. The main advantage of ETES systems is their ability to store large amounts of energy in a compact and relatively inexpensive form. Unlike electrochemical batteries, which can be expensive as storage capacity increases, ETES systems can be designed to store greater than 5 hours of discharge capacity, making them ideal for storing excess electricity from intermittent renewable energy sources. Goals and Objectives The goal of the project was to determine the cost savings from using PCM for TES in the ETES. The higher energy density of the salt slurry compared to the salt should result in smaller TES tank dimensions and therefore lower costs. NREL, through a Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) VELOCTI voucher, was tasked with developing a model of an ETES system using the PowderMet Inc. particle/salt slurry as the storage medium in the System Advisor Model (SAM) framework. NREL was further tasked with using the model to do parametric analysis on the system to determine a range of system costs in terms of LCOE. PowderMet Inc. specified an ETES plant configuration of a 10 MW net power output with 10 hours of thermal e energy storage capacity.
